newsitem.title: BELARUS: FEATURE - Cold hand of Soviet past touches ex-Belarus leader.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cold hand of Soviet past touches ex-Belarus leader.

text.p: Six years ago Belarus was at the vanguard of the democratic drive to destroy the Soviet Union.
Now the man who thought that he, along with the presidents of Russia and Ukraine, had consigned the communist empire to history, has felt the cold hand of the past on his shoulder.

President Alexander Lukashenko's spring crackdown on the opposition caught up with former Belarus leader Stanislav Shushkevich when he was stopped by a policeman on the street on his way to an exhibition in the capital Minsk.
"I told him he was breaking the law by arresting me. But he looked at me as if to say 'I have to feed my family,'" 62-year-old Shushkevich said in an interview in his Minsk flat.
The former physics professor was released after a few hours and then visited by officials seeking a confession that he had attended an unsanctioned protest. He refused to sign.
Flicking through a photograph album full of shots of himself with world leaders he said drily, "and there's the former defence minister, he's a criminal now too".
Shushkevich and ex-defence minister Pavel Kozlovsky are among scores of people targeted by police for protesting against Lukashenko's drive to unite with Russia.

Lukashenko, who often expresses nostalgia for the Soviet Union, portrays the quest for unity to an equally nostalgic population as a step back to the brotherly Soviet past. Critics see it as a fight for a foothold in the Kremlin at the expense of the long-term interests of 10 million Belarussians.
WAYS OF DEALING WITH DISSENT
Lukashenko, whose stance on reforms has scared off Western lending bodies, has old-fashioned ways of dealing with dissent.
He has pulled back from outlawing rallies outright, but the authorities have either banned marching through the streets or restricted routes in recent months.

Protesters have ignored the restrictions at times, leading to clashes with riot police armed with batons, who waded into crowds. Scores of people on both sides have been injured and hundreds of demonstrators, journalists and bystanders arrested.
Shushkevich hates the violence, though he makes appearances at some protests, delighting younger Lukashenko opponents.
"Will we win?" Sergei, 18, with a red-and-white nationalist band tied around his head, asked Shushkevich shyly at a protest to mark the 11th anniversary of the Chernobyl nuclear accident on April 26.
"Of course," Shushkevich replied, patting him on the back and adding in an aside: "The young ones are in the mood to win".
BELARUSSIANS SEEN AS PASSIVE
Teenagers like Sergei used to listen to rock music and scrawl graffiti like their counterparts in Russia.
Now they let off steam at protests, tying bandanas around their faces and taunting police by chanting "menty" short for "militsionery", as interior ministry officials film every move.
But, unlike the students in Belgrade who forced Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to respect democracy, opposition protests in Minsk usually muster only a few thousand.

Famed for their passivity, Belarussians, many of them wooed by Lukashenko's populist rhetoric, are also seen as unlikely to go the way of Albania and take to arms to remove the president, who has a virtual stranglehold on all branches of power.
Shushkevich said appearances could be deceptive. "Did anyone ever say the Albanians weren't peaceful?".

But for now at least the opposition is cautious -- nationalist Popular Front activists even warned their comrades to keep off the grass at the Chernobyl anniversary protest which attracted about 30,000 people.
KREMLIN HAS THE POWER TO CONTROL LUKASHENKO
The protesters suspect the only real influence on Lukashenko is the Kremlin, which has stayed silent about the country's record on democracy and reforms.
If he wanted, Russian President Boris Yeltsin could turn off the tap on energy supplies, or further isolate Lukashenko by joining Western leaders in slamming his style of rule.
But Moscow stayed mute as Lukashenko, a former farm boss who rose to power amid an anti-corruption drive which saw off Shushkevich in 1994, has steadily increased his powers.

Lukashenko's allegations against the then government included accusing Shushkevich of working for Western intelligence agencies -- a charge dismissed by the country's own secret service which is still called the KGB.

Lukashenko's pleas to join Russia, equally smitten with nostalgia for the Soviet superpower, are hard to resist and his authoritarian rule is a convenient model to hold up to the West when it shows reluctance to help finance Russian reforms.
It was only when Lukashenko turned his attention to the Kremlin that Russia put its foot down, and then only at the last minute.
Lukashenko had proposed a Union Treaty with Russia giving him four seats in an eight-seat joint council which had the power to take important decisions about both countries' future.

"Under cover of integration he tried to seize power from Yeltsin. Yeltsin was sick but he didn't lose his mind," Shushkevich said, referring to the health problems which have dogged the 66-year-old Russian president.

Russian liberals managed to water down the treaty so that when Yeltsin signed it on April 2, it bore startling resemblance to a commonwealth deal signed a year ago. "All they did was change the word commonwealth to union," Shushkevich said.
SHUSHKEVICH'S ROLE
Shushkevich, a social democrat who almost single-handedly fought for reforms as Belarus' first post-Soviet leader, seemed at a loss to explain the developments of the past few years.

Critics say with hindsight that Shushkevich, a physicist who never held a senior Communist Party post and who now travels Europe delivering lectures, was partly to blame for the country's slide to near-pariah status.
"He didn't want power. He didn't know what to do with it once it was in his hands. He's a good man, but he's no politician," said a fellow Lukashenko opponent.
If this is true, Shushkevich got what he wanted.

He lost his political clout completely last year when Lukashenko disbanded parliament after ignoring constitutional court rulings and parliamentary votes to hold a controversial referendum which he won by a landslide.
Shushkevich and several dozen other deputies who refused to join the new, overwhelmingly pro-presidential chamber, formed an alternative one which has no power except to convey ideas.

It is a far cry from the days when Shushkevich chatted with U.S. President Bill Clinton, or the high-point of his political career in December 1991, when he, Yeltsin and Ukrainian President Leonid Kravchuk signed away the Soviet Union.

Asked if he planned take part in presidential elections, set back to November 2002 since Lukashenko's new constitution re-started the timer on his five-year term, Shushkevich shrugged. "I couldn't do a worse job than Lukashenko".
